note: Paul is sure God will finish the good work He began in His people. In Ephesians he shows one way God does it: He gives leaders to prepare His people for service so the church grows up.
Both picture a believer's whole life as an offering to God. Paul urges us to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice; Peter calls believers a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices.
Joshua reminds Israel that one of them could chase off a thousand because the Lord fought for them. The psalm prays to God as King, the one who gives His people victory.
Both ask what anyone can do against people God is helping. Hebrews says the Lord is our helper, so we need not fear; Paul asks who can stand against us if God is for us.
Both are promises of a new covenant in which God works inside His people: Isaiah says His Spirit and His words will stay with them for good, and Ezekiel says God will wash them clean and renew them.
Both connect a changed mind with knowing God's will. Paul says a renewed mind is able to test and approve what God wants, and urges the Ephesians to understand what the Lord's will is.
Samuel tells Saul that obeying God matters more than offering sacrifices. Centuries later Jeremiah says the same: what God first asked of Israel was to listen to His voice.
Both describe God holding people up. In Isaiah God promises to strengthen and uphold His people; the psalm praises the Lord who lifts up all who fall and are bowed down.

Both link waiting on the Lord with strength and hope. Isaiah says those who wait for Him will renew their strength; the psalmist is sure he will see God's goodness and tells himself to wait for the Lord.
Isaiah promises that God's people will never be put to shame. Peter takes up the same promise for everyone who trusts in Jesus, the cornerstone God has laid.
Both encourage asking God with confidence. Jesus tells His disciples to ask and keep asking, and says He chose them to bear lasting fruit so the Father will give what they ask in His name.
Both say that with the Lord on our side there is no one to fear. Hebrews says the Lord is my helper; the psalm says the Lord is my light and my salvation, so whom shall I fear?
Both warn against relying on ourselves to find the way. Proverbs says to trust the Lord rather than our own understanding; Jeremiah admits that people cannot direct their own steps.
Ezekiel records God's promise to give His people a new heart and a new spirit. Paul calls believers to be transformed by the renewing of their minds, the change God promised.
Both say God's gift drives out fear. Paul says God has not given us a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-control; John says perfect love casts out fear.

Both tell God's people to watch over their inner life. Proverbs says to guard your heart because everything flows from it; Moses tells Israel to watch themselves closely so they do not forget what God has done.
Both speak of how lasting and reliable God's word is. Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away but His words will not; Proverbs says every word of God is proven true.
Both warn against going the way of the wicked. The psalm calls blessed the person who does not walk in their counsel; Proverbs says not to set foot on their path.
Both show God overturning human plans. The psalm says the Lord brings the plans of the nations to nothing; in Isaiah He frustrates the signs of false prophets and makes the wise look foolish.
Both promise that opposition will not win because God is with His people. God tells Jeremiah his enemies will fight him but not overcome him; Paul asks who can be against us if God is for us.

Both warn against trusting our own cleverness. Proverbs says not to lean on our own understanding; Paul says anyone who thinks he is wise by this world's standards should become a fool to become truly wise.
Jesus asks His disciples if they have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear. He echoes the words Jeremiah used for a people who would not understand God.
Both invite bold prayer. Jesus says to ask and it will be given; in John He adds that those who remain in Him, with His words in them, can ask what they wish.
Both trace everything back to God's love. John says God so loved the world that He gave His Son; Paul says God loved us and by His grace gave us eternal comfort and good hope.
Both assure believers that work done for God is not wasted. Paul says our labor in the Lord is never in vain; Hebrews says God will not forget the love His people have shown.
Both promise God's peace to those who trust Him. Isaiah speaks of perfect peace for the mind fixed on God; Paul says God's peace will guard our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
Both use water to picture God's blessing on His people. Isaiah promises water on thirsty ground and God's Spirit on their children; Joel sees a spring flowing out from the Lord's house.
Both say God's power does not depend on numbers. Joshua says one Israelite could rout a thousand; Jonathan says nothing can stop the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.
Hebrews repeats God's new covenant promise to write His laws on His people's hearts. Paul describes the believers in Corinth as that promise come true: a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts.
Both state why Jesus came. He says He came to call sinners, not the righteous; after meeting Zacchaeus He says He came to seek and save the lost.
Both call God's people His temple. Paul tells the Corinthians twice that God lives among them by His Spirit, so they belong to Him alone.
Both teach that God reverses pride. Proverbs says pride brings a person low while the humble gain honor; Jesus says everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the humble will be exalted.
